frame-u01.text: KP08 L2 regularization and weight decay

scene-u01-pnew1-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew1-25.text: Where does an $\ell_2$ penalty push the solution? First write the objective

scene-u01-pnew1-30.name: text#30
scene-u01-pnew1-30.text: The $\tfrac12$ in front only cancels the $2$ when differentiating.

scene-u01-pnew1-32.name: text#32
scene-u01-pnew1-32.text: This unit's $\alpha$ = KP07's $2\alpha$ (because of the extra $\tfrac12$).

scene-u01-pnew1-61.name: text#61
scene-u01-pnew1-61.text: The same $\alpha$, yet a factor of $2$ apart between units!

scene-u01-pnew2-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew2-25.text: Near the optimum, view $J$ as a parabola

scene-u01-pnew3-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew3-25.text: Check against KP07: this formula gives exactly $w^{\dagger}=w^{\ast}/(1+\alpha_K)$

scene-u01-pnew3-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew3-26.text: KP07's example $J=(w-w^{\ast})^2$ has second derivative $2$, so $\lambda=2$; this unit's $\alpha=2\alpha_K$.

scene-u01-pnew3-48.name: text#48
scene-u01-pnew3-48.text: At $\alpha_K=0.5,\,1,\,3$ the factors are $0.6667,\,0.5,\,0.25$: exactly KP07.

scene-u01-pnew4-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew4-25.text: With many parameters: each direction has its own steepness and its own shrink factor

scene-u01-pnew4-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew4-26.text: The last section's formula applies direction by direction, not one multiplier for every weight.

scene-u01-pnew4-29.name: text#29
scene-u01-pnew4-29.text:
one step toward the origin makes $J$ jump;
the penalty saved cannot make up for it.

scene-u01-pnew4-33.name: text#33
scene-u01-pnew4-33.text:
going far barely changes $J$;
the penalty wins.

scene-u01-pnew4-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew4-38.text: Steep directions shrink less, flat ones more: each direction on its own.

scene-u01-pnew5-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew5-25.text: Work it out with two directions: $\lambda_1=4$, $\lambda_2=0.5$, $\alpha=1$

scene-u01-pnew5-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew5-26.text: Suppose $\mathbf x^{\ast}$ has components $(10,\,10)$ along the two directions.

scene-u01-pnew5-58.name: text#58
scene-u01-pnew5-58.text: One $\alpha$: the steep direction shrinks from $10$ to $8$, the flat one from $10$ to $3.33$.

scene-u01-pnew6-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew6-25.text: In the picture: the flatter the ellipse direction ($J$ flatter), the harder it is squeezed

scene-u01-pnew6-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew6-26.text: Blue contours are $J$ centred at $\mathbf x^{\ast}$; axes are the two directions $\mathbf u_1,\mathbf u_2$.

scene-u01-pnew6-46.name: text#46
scene-u01-pnew6-46.text:
along the long axis $\mathbf u_2$ ($J$ flat) it shrinks a lot: $10\to 3.33$
along the short axis $\mathbf u_1$ ($J$ steep) a little: $10\to 8$

scene-u01-pnew6-48.name: text#48
scene-u01-pnew6-48.text: gold: the contour through $\mathbf x^{\dagger}$ ($J\approx 19.1$); at the origin $J(\mathbf 0)=225$.

scene-u01-pnew6-50.name: text#50
scene-u01-pnew6-50.text: The flatter the ellipse direction ($J$ flatter), the harder it is squeezed.

scene-u01-pnew7-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew7-25.text: Shrink factors against $\alpha$: the flat direction drops much faster

scene-u01-pnew7-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew7-26.text: Both start at $1$ and fall, yet stay above $0$.

scene-u01-pnew7-61.name: text#61
scene-u01-pnew7-61.text: $\alpha=1$: $0.800$ and $0.333$, the two factors just computed.

scene-u01-pnew7-63.name: text#63
scene-u01-pnew7-63.text: $\alpha=10$: $0.286$ and $0.048$ remain. The curves stay above $0$.

scene-u01-pnew7-85.name: text#85
scene-u01-pnew7-85.text: Every factor is positive: shrinking never lands exactly on zero.

scene-u01-pnew8-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew8-25.text: What remains per direction adds up to the model's "effective" degrees of freedom

scene-u01-pnew8-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew8-26.text: Definition: the effective number of parameters.

scene-u01-pnew8-30.name: text#30
scene-u01-pnew8-30.text:
$\alpha=0$: every factor is $1$,
df equals the number of parameters (all free).

scene-u01-pnew8-34.name: text#34
scene-u01-pnew8-34.text: In the example at $\alpha=1$: $0.8+0.3333=1.1333$. Of the original $2$ parameters about $1.13$ remain.

scene-u01-pnew8-36.name: text#36
scene-u01-pnew8-36.text: The sum of the factors is "how many effective parameters remain".

scene-u01-pnew9-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew9-25.text: As $\alpha$ grows, the two factors stacked into df keep shrinking

scene-u01-pnew9-59.name: text#59
scene-u01-pnew9-59.text: The larger $\alpha$, the fewer effective parameters, the less it follows the noise.

scene-u01-pnew10-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew10-25.text: The effective parameter count does not fall linearly

scene-u01-pnew10-65.name: text#65
scene-u01-pnew10-65.text:
$\alpha$ from $0$ to $1$: drops $0.87$
from $1$ to $10$: only another $0.80$

scene-u01-pnew10-67.name: text#67
scene-u01-pnew10-67.text: df is the sum of all factors and usually falls non-linearly.

scene-u01-pnew10-89.name: text#89
scene-u01-pnew10-89.text: A little $\alpha$ shrinks a lot at first, then ever more slowly.

scene-u01-pnew11-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew11-25.text: Every factor is above $0$: $\ell_2$ never selects features automatically

scene-u01-pnew11-49.name: text#49
scene-u01-pnew11-49.text: (conceptual: all six components shrink, none reaches zero)

scene-u01-pnew11-78.name: text#78
scene-u01-pnew11-78.text: Want exact zeros? Switch the penalty.

scene-u01-pnew11-80.name: text#80
scene-u01-pnew11-80.text: So $\ell_2$ does not select features automatically.

scene-u01-pnew12-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew12-25.text: Applied to a network: an $\ell_2$ penalty on all weights is weight decay

scene-u01-pnew12-34.name: text#34
scene-u01-pnew12-34.text: Why "decay"? Next page: every gradient step first shrinks the weights a little.

scene-u01-pnew12-56.name: text#56
scene-u01-pnew12-56.text: Weight decay = an $\ell_2$ penalty on all weights $\mathbf w$.

scene-u01-pnew13-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew13-25.text: Each step: first multiply the weights by a factor just below 1, then correct by the gradient

scene-u01-pnew13-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew13-26.text: One gradient-descent step with learning rate $\eta$.

scene-u01-pnew13-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew13-28.text: $\mathbf w\leftarrow\mathbf w-\eta\big(\nabla J+\alpha\mathbf w\big)=(1-\eta\alpha)\,\mathbf w-\eta\,\nabla J(\mathbf w)$

scene-u01-pnew13-32.name: text#32
scene-u01-pnew13-32.text: ② then correct by the data gradient $-\eta\nabla J$

scene-u01-pnew13-41.name: text#41
scene-u01-pnew13-41.text: Without decay it is $2-0.1=1.9$: decay shrinks the weight $0.1=\eta\alpha w$ more.

scene-u01-pnew14-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew14-25.text: Why does shrinking weights help networks? Large weights push activations into saturation

scene-u01-pnew14-45.name: text#45
scene-u01-pnew14-45.text: The larger $w$, the more inputs saturate: the output sticks to $\pm1$ and stops changing.

scene-u01-pnew15-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew15-25.text: Three weight sizes: the only difference is one weight

scene-u01-pnew15-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew15-26.text: $\tanh(wx)$; the red bands are the saturated region $|\tanh|>0.95$.

scene-u01-pnew15-52.name: text#52
scene-u01-pnew15-52.text: green $w=0.5$: stays inside the band, never saturates.

scene-u01-pnew15-54.name: text#54
scene-u01-pnew15-54.text: blue $w=1$: touches the red band beyond $|x|>1.832$.

scene-u01-pnew15-58.name: text#58
scene-u01-pnew15-58.text: Weight decay keeps the network in the near-linear region, which usually generalises better.

scene-u01-pnew16-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew16-25.text: $\ell_2$ only shrinks, never zeroes; how to get exact zeros?

scene-u01-pnew16-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew16-26.text: Automatic feature selection needs exact zeros.

scene-u01-pnew16-68.name: text#68
scene-u01-pnew16-68.text:
KP09
L1 and the
soft threshold

scene-u01-pnew16-70.name: text#70
scene-u01-pnew16-70.text: The answer is KP09: switch to an $\ell_1$ penalty.

steps.label: KP08 L2 regularization and weight decay
KP08 · 1/16
steps.speakerNotes: KP07 ended by asking where an ℓ2 penalty pushes the solution. First the objective: J̃(x) = J(x) + (α/2)x².

steps.label: KP08 · 1/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: KP07 ended by asking where an ℓ2 penalty pushes the solution. First the objective: J̃(x) = J(x) + (α/2)x².

steps.label: KP08 · 1/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The ½ in front only cancels the 2 when differentiating.

steps.label: KP08 · 1/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: So this unit's α equals KP07's 2α; keep this in mind.

steps.label: KP08 · 2/16
steps.speakerNotes: Near the unregularized optimum x*, J is approximated by an upward parabola with steepness λ: steep means large λ, flat small λ.

steps.label: KP08 · 2/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Near the unregularized optimum x*, J is approximated by an upward parabola with steepness λ: steep means large λ, flat small λ.

steps.label: KP08 · 2/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Substitute into J̃ and set the derivative to zero: λ(x − x*) + αx = 0.

steps.label: KP08 · 2/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: So x† = λ/(λ + α) · x*: x* times a shrink factor between 0 and 1. At α = 0 the factor is 1; the larger α, the smaller the factor.

steps.label: KP08 · 3/16
steps.speakerNotes: KP07's one-weight example J = (w − w*)² has second derivative 2, so λ = 2; the penalty α_K w² is (2α_K/2) w², so this unit's α = 2α_K.

steps.label: KP08 · 3/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: KP07's one-weight example J = (w − w*)² has second derivative 2, so λ = 2; the penalty α_K w² is (2α_K/2) w², so this unit's α = 2α_K.

steps.label: KP08 · 3/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The factor is 2/(2 + 2α_K) = 1/(1 + α_K), exactly KP07's w† = w*/(1 + α_K).

steps.label: KP08 · 3/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: At α_K = 0.5, 1, 3 it is 0.6667, 0.5000, 0.2500. (x* taken as 1; the stars sit at these positions to scale.)

steps.label: KP08 · 4/16
steps.speakerNotes: With many parameters J has a different steepness λ in each direction; the last formula applies direction by direction.

steps.label: KP08 · 4/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: With many parameters J has a different steepness λ in each direction; the last formula applies direction by direction.

steps.label: KP08 · 4/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Steep (λ ≫ α): one step toward the origin makes J jump and the penalty saved cannot compensate, so it barely moves, factor near 1.

steps.label: KP08 · 4/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Flat (λ ≪ α): going far barely changes J, the penalty wins and squeezes hard, factor near 0; at λ = α the factor is exactly 1/2.

steps.label: KP08 · 5/16
steps.speakerNotes: Direction 1, steep, λ = 4, α = 1: 4/(4 + 1) = 0.8, losing only 20%.

steps.label: KP08 · 5/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Direction 1, steep, λ = 4, α = 1: 4/(4 + 1) = 0.8, losing only 20%.

steps.label: KP08 · 5/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Direction 2, flat, λ = 0.5: 0.5/(0.5 + 1) = 0.3333, losing about 67%.

steps.label: KP08 · 6/16
steps.speakerNotes: The blue ellipses are contours of J centred at x* = (10, 10); the u₂ semi-axis is longer because that direction is flatter (λ = 0.5) while u₁ is steeper (λ = 4). (The lecture figure's rotation is omitted; the two directions are used as axes.)

steps.label: KP08 · 6/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The blue ellipses are contours of J centred at x* = (10, 10); the u₂ semi-axis is longer because that direction is flatter (λ = 0.5) while u₁ is steeper (λ = 4). (The lecture figure's rotation is omitted; the two directions are used as axes.)

steps.label: KP08 · 6/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The gold contour passes through x† = (8, 3.33), J's height there; the arrow runs from x* to x†.

steps.label: KP08 · 6/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The grey dashed contour passes through the origin, J(0) = 225. Shrinks a lot along the long axis, little along the short one.

steps.label: KP08 · 7/16
steps.speakerNotes: Blue λ = 4 (steep), red λ = 0.5 (flat): both start at 1 and fall, the flat one much faster.

steps.label: KP08 · 7/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Blue λ = 4 (steep), red λ = 0.5 (flat): both start at 1 and fall, the flat one much faster.

steps.label: KP08 · 7/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: On the dashed line α = 1 the two points are 0.800 and 0.333, the factors just computed.

steps.label: KP08 · 7/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: At α = 10 they are 0.286 and 0.048. The curves stay above 0: shrinking never lands exactly on zero.

steps.label: KP08 · 8/16
steps.speakerNotes: What remains per direction adds up to the model's effective degrees of freedom: df(α) is the sum of all shrink factors.

steps.label: KP08 · 8/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: What remains per direction adds up to the model's effective degrees of freedom: df(α) is the sum of all shrink factors.

steps.label: KP08 · 8/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: At α = 0 every factor is 1 and df equals the number of parameters; as α → ∞ every factor → 0 and df → 0.

steps.label: KP08 · 8/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: In the example at α = 1: 0.8 + 0.3333 = 1.1333: of the original 2 parameters about 1.13 remain.

steps.label: KP08 · 9/16
steps.speakerNotes: Each bar stacks two factors: blue is direction 1 (λ = 4), red direction 2 (λ = 0.5).

steps.label: KP08 · 9/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Each bar stacks two factors: blue is direction 1 (λ = 4), red direction 2 (λ = 0.5).

steps.label: KP08 · 9/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: This is the evidence that ℓ2 really lowers complexity: the larger α, the fewer effective parameters, the less it follows the noise.

steps.label: KP08 · 10/16
steps.speakerNotes: The left end 2.000 is no regularization; the labelled points are 1.133, 0.714, 0.333.

steps.label: KP08 · 10/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The left end 2.000 is no regularization; the labelled points are 1.133, 0.714, 0.333.

steps.label: KP08 · 10/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The curve is not a straight line: α from 0 to 1 loses 0.87, from 1 to 10 only another 0.80.

steps.label: KP08 · 10/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: df is the sum of all factors and usually falls non-linearly.

steps.label: KP08 · 11/16
steps.speakerNotes: Every factor λ/(λ + α) is strictly above 0 for any λ > 0 and finite α.

steps.label: KP08 · 11/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Every factor λ/(λ + α) is strictly above 0 for any λ > 0 and finite α.

steps.label: KP08 · 11/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: ℓ2 shrinks all directions but never makes a component exactly zero, so it does not select features automatically. (Bar heights are a conceptual sketch.)

steps.label: KP08 · 11/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Exact zeros need a different penalty: KP09.

steps.label: KP08 · 12/16
steps.speakerNotes: Putting ℓ2 on all network weights w is weight decay: J̃(w) = J(w) + (α/2)‖w‖₂².

steps.label: KP08 · 12/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Putting ℓ2 on all network weights w is weight decay: J̃(w) = J(w) + (α/2)‖w‖₂².

steps.label: KP08 · 12/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Its gradient is ∇J̃ = ∇J + αw.

steps.label: KP08 · 12/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Why decay? The next page shows one gradient-descent step.

steps.label: KP08 · 13/16
steps.speakerNotes: One step: w ← w − η(∇J + αw) = (1 − ηα)w − η∇J(w).

steps.label: KP08 · 13/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: One step: w ← w − η(∇J + αw) = (1 − ηα)w − η∇J(w).

steps.label: KP08 · 13/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Two parts: first multiply the weights by a factor just below 1, (1 − ηα), a bit of decay each step; then correct by the usual gradient −η∇J.

steps.label: KP08 · 13/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Added example: η = 0.1, α = 0.5, w = 2, ∂J/∂w = 1: (1 − 0.05)·2 − 0.1·1 = 1.8, checked with 2 − 0.1(1 + 0.5·2) = 1.8; without decay 1.9, so 0.1 = ηαw more. In PyTorch this is the optimizer's weight_decay argument (not run in this environment).

steps.label: KP08 · 14/16
steps.speakerNotes: The source's reason: large weights push the nonlinear activation into its saturated region. For tanh(wx), call |tanh| > 0.95 saturated; since tanh(1.832) = 0.95, |wx| > 1.832 is saturated.

steps.label: KP08 · 14/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The source's reason: large weights push the nonlinear activation into its saturated region. For tanh(wx), call |tanh| > 0.95 saturated; since tanh(1.832) = 0.95, |wx| > 1.832 is saturated.

steps.label: KP08 · 14/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: w = 4: |x| > 0.458, 84.7%. (Computed.) With large w the curve turns sharply near 0 and flattens on both sides, so gradients vanish on the flat parts.

steps.label: KP08 · 15/16
steps.speakerNotes: The green curve (w = 0.5) stays inside the band, never saturating.

steps.label: KP08 · 15/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The green curve (w = 0.5) stays inside the band, never saturating.

steps.label: KP08 · 15/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The blue curve (w = 1) touches the red band beyond |x| > 1.832.

steps.label: KP08 · 15/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The orange curve (w = 4) sticks to ±1 already beyond |x| > 0.458. The three differ only in one weight. Weight decay keeps the network near-linear, which usually generalises better.

steps.label: KP08 · 16/16
steps.speakerNotes: ℓ2 only shrinks and never zeroes.

steps.label: KP08 · 16/16 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: ℓ2 only shrinks and never zeroes.

steps.label: KP08 · 16/16 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: What if we want exact zeros, i.e. automatic feature selection?

steps.label: KP08 · 16/16 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The answer is an ℓ1 penalty: the topic of KP09.
